period_summary: Citations are heavily concentrated in the 2nd–4th centuries CE, driven by christological controversy. The passage became a central proof-text in debates with Jews over messianic prophecy and the virgin birth, making it one of the most frequently cited OT verses in early Christian literature.

citations.cited_text: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν, καὶ καλέσουσιν τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουήλ (Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel)
citations.text_form_note: Justin's citation consistently uses 'παρθένος' (virgin) matching LXX against MT 'עלמה' (young woman). The future tense 'ἕξει καὶ τέξεται' and the plural 'καλέσουσιν' align precisely with LXX Isaiah tradition as attested in codices.
citations.theological_use: Justin deploys this text polemically against Trypho to prove that Isaiah prophesied a virgin birth, not merely a young woman bearing a child. He argues the LXX's 'παρθένος' is the authentic reading and that Jewish interlocutors have falsified the text by reading 'young woman' to evade the christological claim.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's insistence on the LXX reading suggests that by the mid-2nd century, competing Greek or Hebrew text forms were already circulating in Jewish-Christian debate contexts.

citations.cited_text: Ecce virgo in utero accipiet et pariet filium (Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son)
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus cites via Old Latin ('virgo') which presupposes Greek 'παρθένος' from LXX. He explicitly contrasts this with Theodotion and Aquila's renderings ('young woman'), demonstrating awareness of competing translations. His text matches the LXX tradition as witnessed in Christian manuscripts.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses Isa 7:14 to defend the virgin birth against both Jewish objections and Gnostic reinterpretations. He insists the prophecy requires a miraculous conception and that alternative translations are evasions designed to undermine Christian doctrine.
citations.transmission_implication: Irenaeus's awareness of Aquila/Theodotion variants reveals that by c. 180 CE, revised Greek translations closer to the Hebrew were competing with the Christian LXX tradition in apologetic contexts.

citations.cited_text: Ecce virgo concipiet in utero et pariet filium (Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son)
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Old Latin citation 'virgo' reflects underlying LXX 'παρθένος'. He argues explicitly that 'virgo' not 'iuvenis' (young woman) is the correct reading, engaging directly with the Hebrew-text tradition known through Jewish debate partners.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian wields Isa 7:14 against Marcion to prove the OT foretold Christ's virgin birth, thus establishing continuity between the Creator God and the Redeemer. He also uses it against Jewish interpreters, arguing they have obscured the plain meaning to avoid acknowledging Jesus.
citations.transmission_implication: Tertullian's Latin text presupposes a stable LXX-based tradition in North Africa, transmitted through early Latin translations by the late 2nd century.

citations.cited_text: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν (Behold, the virgin in the womb shall have and bear a son)
citations.text_form_note: Origen's citation matches the LXX column of his Hexapla. He explicitly discusses the Hebrew 'עלמה' and Aquila's translation 'νεᾶνις', but defends the LXX 'παρθένος' as the inspired Christian text. His awareness of textual plurality is unmatched in this period.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses Isa 7:14 to defend the virgin birth against Celsus's mockery, arguing that the LXX's inspired rendering 'παρθένος' was providentially ordained for Gentile Christians. He subordinates Hebrew fidelity to theological necessity.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexapla work reveals that multiple Greek text forms (LXX, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) coexisted in 3rd-century scholarly circles, but the LXX dominated liturgical and doctrinal use.

citations.cited_text: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται καὶ τέξεται υἱόν (Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son)
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius cites from the LXX tradition, though with minor variation ('λήψεται' for 'ἕξει', both meaning 'shall have/conceive'). He inherited Origen's text-critical awareness but defaults to the LXX for apologetic purposes. The reading 'λήψεται' appears in some LXX witnesses and may reflect Hexaplaric influence.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius employs Isa 7:14 as a proof-text for the historical fulfillment of prophecy in Christ's birth, part of his broader apologetic demonstrating the rational credibility of Christianity through fulfilled OT predictions.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius's citation reflects the dominance of LXX-based texts in 4th-century Caesarea, even as minor textual variants ('λήψεται' vs 'ἕξει') circulated within that tradition.

citations.cited_text: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν (Behold, the virgin shall have in the womb and bear a son)
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius's citation is a verbatim match with the standard Alexandrian LXX text of Isaiah. He shows no awareness of textual debate; the LXX reading is assumed as authoritative and unproblematic for his theological argument.
citations.theological_use: Athanasius uses Isa 7:14 to establish the dual reality of Christ's humanity (born of a virgin) and divinity (Incarnation of the Logos). The virgin birth is non-negotiable for his soteriology: only God-made-man can deify humanity.
citations.transmission_implication: By the mid-4th century in Alexandria, the LXX text of Isa 7:14 had achieved canonical stability in Christian circles, with no trace of Hebrew-based alternatives in ecclesiastical literature.

citations.cited_text: ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν, καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουήλ (Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel)
citations.text_form_note: Cyril's citation follows the LXX tradition with the singular 'καλέσεις' (you shall call) variant attested in some LXX manuscripts, against the more common 'καλέσουσιν' (they shall call). This reflects textual fluidity within the LXX tradition itself.
citations.theological_use: Cyril uses Isa 7:14 in catechetical instruction to teach candidates for baptism the scriptural basis of Christ's virgin birth. The name Emmanuel ('God with us') underscores the Incarnation's significance for salvation history.
citations.transmission_implication: Cyril's variant ('καλέσεις' singular) attests to ongoing scribal variation within the LXX textual tradition in 4th-century Palestine, even as the core reading ('παρθένος') remained stable.

citations.cited_text: Ecce virgo concipiet... Hebrew has 'almah', which Aquila and Symmachus translate as 'young woman', but the Seventy rightly rendered 'virgin' for theological reasons.
citations.text_form_note: Jerome is unique in his critical engagement with the Hebrew text. He acknowledges 'עלמה' does not strictly mean 'virgin' but defends the LXX's 'virgo/παρθένος' on theological and apostolic grounds. His Vulgate retains 'virgo' despite his Hebrew knowledge, showing deference to Christian tradition.
citations.theological_use: Jerome uses Isa 7:14 to defend the virgin birth while also educating Latin readers about the Hebrew original. He navigates between textual fidelity to the Hebrew and doctrinal fidelity to the apostolic LXX-based tradition, privileging the latter.
citations.transmission_implication: Jerome's testimony reveals that by the late 4th century, Christian scholars knew the LXX's 'virgin' was an interpretation rather than a literal rendering of 'עלמה', yet the LXX reading was retained as doctrinally authoritative.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation history of Isa 7:14 reveals near-universal dependence on the LXX tradition (Greek 'παρθένος' = virgin, Latin 'virgo') from the 2nd through 5th centuries, with no Church Father preferring the Hebrew 'עלמה' (young woman) or proto-MT readings. This uniformity reflects the LXX's status as the Christian Old Testament and the theological necessity of the 'virgin' reading for defending the virgin birth against Jewish and pagan critics. However, citations also attest awareness of competing Greek translations (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) that rendered 'עלמה' more literally as 'young woman'/'νεᾶνις', indicating that by the late 2nd century multiple text forms circulated in apologetic contexts. Internal LXX variants (e.g., 'καλέσεις' vs 'καλέσουσιν', 'λήψεται' vs 'ἕξει') demonstrate scribal fluidity within the Christian textual tradition, but the core reading 'παρθένος' remained stable and doctrinally non-negotiable. Jerome's testimony confirms that Christian scholars recognized the LXX's interpretive character but subordinated textual-critical precision to theological tradition, cementing the LXX reading as canonical for Western and Eastern Christianity.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from the 2nd to 5th centuries consistently cite Isaiah 7:14 using the Greek Septuagint translation, which reads 'virgin' rather than the Hebrew 'young woman'. Even when Church Fathers like Origen and Jerome knew the Hebrew text and alternative Greek translations that said 'young woman', they defended the 'virgin' reading as theologically necessary for Christian belief in Jesus's virgin birth. This shows the Septuagint became the authoritative Old Testament for Christians, sometimes prioritizing doctrinal tradition over strict translation of the Hebrew.

notable_variants.reading: παρθένος (parthenos, virgin) vs Hebrew עלמה (almah, young woman)
notable_variants.significance: This is the single most significant textual variant in the OT for Christian doctrine. The LXX's 'virgin' enabled a messianic-christological reading central to the virgin birth tradition, whereas the Hebrew 'young woman' is semantically neutral regarding virginity. The universal patristic preference for 'παρθένος' reveals how the LXX shaped Christian theological exegesis independently of the Hebrew text.

notable_variants.reading: καλέσουσιν (they shall call) vs καλέσεις (you shall call)
notable_variants.significance: This minor variant within the LXX tradition (plural vs singular) reflects scribal variation in transmission but does not affect the core theological point. It demonstrates that even within the dominant LXX textual tradition, copying introduced grammatical variants that fathers cited without consistency, suggesting liturgical and manuscript diversity.

notable_variants.reading: ἕξει (hexei, shall have) vs λήψεται (lēpsetai, shall take/receive)
notable_variants.significance: Both verbs convey conception but with slight semantic difference ('have' vs 'take'). Eusebius's use of 'λήψεται' may reflect Hexaplaric or recensional influence, possibly from Origen's work. This variant shows that Caesarean scholars had access to text forms influenced by Hexaplaric scholarship, creating minor divergences from the mainstream Alexandrian LXX.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX's 'Virgin' Reading Became Christian Doctrinal Canon
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The unanimous patristic attestation of 'παρθένος' (virgin) over against the Hebrew 'עלמה' (young woman) reveals that the LXX was not merely a translation but the Christian Old Testament, whose theological readings achieved canonical status independent of the Hebrew text. Even when patristic scholars like Origen and Jerome became aware that 'עלמה' did not strictly denote virginity, they defended the LXX on theological grounds, arguing it was divinely inspired for Christian use. This demonstrates that textual transmission in early Christianity was driven by doctrinal necessity as much as by manuscript fidelity, and that Isa 7:14's text history cannot be understood apart from its role in christological controversy.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Church Fathers universally cited Isaiah 7:14 with the Greek word for 'virgin', even after some learned the Hebrew word meant 'young woman'. This shows early Christians treated the Greek Old Testament as scripture in its own right, shaped by theological conviction about Jesus's virgin birth rather than strict translation of Hebrew.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis is broadly accurate on the main textual-critical landscape of Isa 7:14, but contains several specific citation references and quoted Greek/Latin forms that need verification, and some chapter/section numbers appear imprecise or wrong.

flagged_claims.reason: Book 3.21 of Against Heresies does discuss Isa 7:14, but it does not extend through section 10; the standard divisions go to 3.21.10 in some editions but the citation of Isa 7:14 is concentrated in 3.21.1–4. The range is overstated.
Isa 7:14 is more commonly cited in On the Incarnation ch. 33 (within the prophetic proofs section), not ch. 8. This chapter reference appears incorrect.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius cites 'λήψεται' for 'ἕξει' in Demonstratio Evangelica 7.1
flagged_claims.reason: The specific Greek verb form attributed to Eusebius needs verification; while Demonstratio Evangelica book 7 does treat Isa 7:14, the precise wording quoted here may be a reconstruction rather than a verified citation.

flagged_claims.claim: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures 12.21, with variant 'καλέσεις' (singular)
flagged_claims.reason: Cat. Lect. 12 does discuss the virgin birth and Isa 7:14, but the specific section 12.21 and the singular 'καλέσεις' variant attribution requires verification; standard LXX and most patristic citations have 'καλέσουσιν' or 'καλέσεις' depending on the manuscript, and assigning a specific variant to Cyril at 12.21 is precise enough to risk error.

flagged_claims.claim: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho ch. 43, 67, 71, 84
flagged_claims.reason: Justin does cite Isa 7:14 multiple times in the Dialogue, and chs. 43, 66-68, 71, and 84 are plausible loci, but the exact list should be verified; ch. 71 in particular relates to Justin's accusation that Jews altered scripture rather than a direct Isa 7:14 quotation.

Justin's citations of Isa 7:14 actually vary; in some places he reads 'καλέσεις' (you shall call, matching MT 2nd singular) and in others reflects different forms. The claim of 'plural καλέσουσιν' aligning 'precisely with LXX' oversimplifies; LXX itself reads 'καλέσεις' in major witnesses.

Letter 57 is on the best method of translation, but Jerome's most famous discussion of almah/parthenos is in his Commentary on Isaiah and in Adversus Helvidium, not principally in Ep. 57.7. The cited text appears paraphrased rather than quoted.
Adv. Marc. 3.13 does treat Isa 7:14, but the cited Latin form should be verified against Tertullian's actual wording, which often differs from later Vulgate phrasing.

safe_claims: LXX reads παρθένος while MT reads עלמה
Aquila and Symmachus rendered עלמה with νεᾶνις rather than παρθένος
Patristic writers overwhelmingly relied on the LXX reading for christological argument
Jerome was aware of the Hebrew almah and the alternative Greek translations but retained 'virgo' in the Vulgate
Origen's Hexapla juxtaposed LXX with Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion
Isa 7:14 was a central proof-text in Jewish-Christian polemic from the 2nd century onward
